--- title: "Forward propagation and backpropagation" description: "A network learns its weights by the same walk downhill as any model fitted by gradient descent. Backpropagation finds the slope for every weight at once." order: 2 categories: [neural-networks, optimisation] --- ## A network learns by walking downhill A network finds its weights the way [Gradient descent](../04-how-algorithms-learn/gradient-descent.qmd) found the slopes of a straight line: measure the loss, find which way is downhill for every weight, take a small step, and repeat. The new part is finding the slopes, because a weight in the hidden layer reaches the prediction only through other weights. **Backpropagation** solves this by passing the error back through the network, layer by layer. This page writes a small network out in base R, checks its slopes, and trains it until it beats linear regression. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ## Backpropagation passes the error back layer by layer Each training step has three parts. - **Forward propagation** pushes the inputs through the network, as on [Neurons, layers and activations](what-a-network-is.qmd), and keeps every value on the way: each hidden unit's weighted sum and its value after the bend. It ends in a prediction, and the loss compares the prediction with the observed value. - **Backpropagation** walks the same arrows in reverse. It starts with how far off each prediction was and asks, for each layer in turn, how much the loss would change if that layer's values changed. Each answer gives the slopes of the weights feeding that layer, and is passed one layer further back. - **The step** moves every weight a little way against its slope, as in gradient descent. ::: {.diagram} ![One training step: a forward pass computes the prediction and the loss, a backward pass gives every weight its slope, and gradient descent moves every weight a little way downhill.](img/training-step.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. Forward pass, predict: a small network with two inputs, three hidden units and an output feeds a box comparing the prediction with the observed value, the loss; an arrow runs from the inputs to the loss; push the inputs through and keep every value on the way; it ends in a prediction and a loss. Backward pass, backpropagation: the same network, with an arrow running from the loss back to the weights; pass the error back along the same arrows to each weight; it gives every weight its slope. Step downhill, gradient descent: a U-shaped curve of the loss against one weight, with dots stepping from a start point down to the bottom; move every weight a little way against its slope; repeat until the loss levels off."} ::: The backward pass is quick because the forward pass has already computed everything it needs. Both passes together cost about twice a forward pass, however many weights the network has, which is what makes networks with millions of weights trainable. ## Worked example We predict abundance on a log scale from depth, temperature and chlorophyll, each standardised, with one hidden layer of four units. The hidden units use **tanh**, the S-shaped activation from minus one to one. ### Both passes fit in a few lines of base R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() model_data <- survey |> select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3) |> drop_na() X <- cbind(depth = as.numeric(scale(model_data$depth_m)), temperature = as.numeric(scale(model_data$temperature_c)), chlorophyll = as.numeric(scale(log1p(model_data$chlorophyll_mg_m3)))) y <- log1p(model_data$abundance) n_hidden <- 4 # Small random weights, so the hidden units start different from one another. # The output bias starts at the mean, so the untrained network predicts the # average. initialise <- function(seed) { set.seed(seed) list(W1 = matrix(rnorm(ncol(X) * n_hidden, 0, 0.5), ncol(X), n_hidden), b1 = rep(0, n_hidden), w2 = rnorm(n_hidden, 0, 0.5), b2 = mean(y)) } ``` ::: `W1` and `b1` are the hidden layer's weights and biases, `w2` and `b2` the output's. The weights start random because hidden units that start the same receive the same slopes and stay the same; randomness lets four units learn four different bends. The forward pass is two matrix multiplications and a bend. The loss is the mean squared error from [Loss functions](../04-how-algorithms-learn/loss-functions.qmd). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} forward <- function(par, X) { Z1 <- sweep(X %*% par$W1, 2, par$b1, "+") # weighted sums into the units A1 <- tanh(Z1) # the units' values after the bend list(Z1 = Z1, A1 = A1, prediction = as.numeric(A1 %*% par$w2 + par$b2)) } loss <- function(par, X, y) mean((y - forward(par, X)$prediction)^2) ``` ::: The backward pass starts from the error and works towards the inputs, reusing `A1` from the forward pass at every step. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} backward <- function(par, X, y) { f <- forward(par, X) n <- nrow(X) # How the loss responds to each prediction, passed back through the output # weights, then through the bend (tanh's slope). d_prediction <- -2 * (y - f$prediction) / n d_A1 <- outer(d_prediction, par$w2) d_Z1 <- d_A1 * (1 - f$A1^2) list(W1 = t(X) %*% d_Z1, b1 = colSums(d_Z1), w2 = as.numeric(t(f$A1) %*% d_prediction), b2 = sum(d_prediction)) } par <- initialise(3) gradients <- backward(par, X, y) ``` ::: Each weight's slope is the error arriving at its layer times the value entering it: the output weights' slopes use the hidden units' values, the hidden weights' slopes use the inputs. The activation appears in one line only, as its slope, `1 - A1^2` for tanh. ### Nudging each weight confirms the slopes A slope worked out by hand can be checked by arithmetic: nudge one weight up and down by a tiny amount and see how much the loss moves. If the backward pass is right, the two agree. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} numerical_gradient <- function(par, X, y, eps = 1e-6) { imap(par, \(values, name) { out <- values for (i in seq_along(values)) { up <- par; down <- par up[[name]][i] <- values[i] + eps down[[name]][i] <- values[i] - eps out[i] <- (loss(up, X, y) - loss(down, X, y)) / (2 * eps) } out }) } nudged <- numerical_gradient(par, X, y) check <- tibble(Weights = c("Hidden weights (W1)", "Hidden biases (b1)", "Output weights (w2)", "Output bias (b2)"), `Largest difference` = map_dbl(names(par), \(nm) { max(abs(as.numeric(gradients[[nm]]) - as.numeric(nudged[[nm]]))) })) check |> mutate(`Largest difference` = sprintf("%.1e", `Largest difference`)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|Weights |Largest difference | |:-------------------|:------------------| |Hidden weights (W1) |5.6e-11 | |Hidden biases (b1) |3.8e-11 | |Output weights (w2) |5.1e-11 | |Output bias (b2) |1.8e-11 |
::: ::: All 21 slopes agree to 10 decimal places. The nudges cost two forward passes per weight, which is cheap for 21 weights and far too slow for training a large network; the backward pass gets every slope from one pass. Run this check whenever you write a gradient yourself: a wrong one still trains, only to the wrong place. ### The hand-written network overtakes linear regression The training loop runs a forward pass, a backward pass and a step, again and again. Each step here uses all 741 stations. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} train <- function(par, X, y, learning_rate = 0.2, steps = 3000) { history <- numeric(steps) for (step in seq_len(steps)) { gradient <- backward(par, X, y) for (nm in names(par)) { par[[nm]] <- par[[nm]] - learning_rate * gradient[[nm]] } history[step] <- loss(par, X, y) } list(par = par, history = history) } fitted_net <- train(initialise(3), X, y) linear_mse <- mean(resid(lm(y ~ X))^2) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(step = seq_along(fitted_net$history), mse = fitted_net$history) |> ggplot(aes(step, mse)) + geom_hline(yintercept = linear_mse, linetype = "dashed", colour = "#9aa5ad") + geom_line(colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.8) + annotate("text", x = 3000, y = linear_mse, label = "Linear regression ", hjust = 1, vjust = -0.6, size = 3.3, colour = "#77818a") + scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 3000), labels = scales::label_comma()) + labs(x = "Gradient-descent step (log scale)", y = "Training mean squared error") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Training loss over 3,000 gradient-descent steps, against linear regression on the same three inputs. The steps are on a log scale, so the early ones are spread out. After a quick first drop the loss pauses on a plateau, falls again, then improves slowly.](forward-and-backward_files/figure-html/fig-descent-1.png){#fig-descent fig-alt='A line against gradient-descent steps on a log scale from one to three thousand. It falls from about 0.76 at the first step to about 0.69 by step fifty, flattens into a near-horizontal plateau until about step one hundred, falls again to about 0.575 by step three hundred, then declines slowly to about 0.558 at step three thousand, with one small brief spike near step two thousand two hundred. A horizontal dashed line at about 0.68 marks linear regression\'s error; the training curve crosses it at about step eighty.' width=1400} ::: ::: The network overtakes linear regression (mean squared error 0.683) at step 81 and ends at 0.558 after 3,000 steps. It was built from nothing but the two passes above, with every slope checked. Two features of the curve are common in network training. The **plateau** after the first drop is a nearly flat stretch of the loss, where the slopes are tiny and progress pauses; a run stopped there would have looked no better than a straight line. The slow crawl at the end is why training longer rarely rescues a disappointing network. The small spike at step 2,247 is a step that overshot the valley; the loss rose for a moment and recovered. [Training a network](training-a-network.qmd) shows how to choose the learning rate and when to stop. ## Software works out the backward pass for you Real software works out the backward pass automatically from the forward pass, so you never write it. What an engine does with the slopes can differ. The `nnet` package used on these pages passes them to **BFGS**, a search that also tracks how the slopes change from step to step and chooses its own step size, so it needs no learning rate. The bend's slope matters too. Where a tanh or logistic unit's weighted sum is large, the curve is flat and its slope is near zero, so little error passes back through the unit and its weights barely move. In networks with many layers this shrinking compounds, the **vanishing gradient**; ReLU, whose slope is one wherever it is active, is the usual remedy. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it Write $\hat y$ for the predictions, $L = \frac{1}{n}\sum (y - \hat y)^2$ for the loss, $Z_1 = XW_1 + b_1$ and $A_1 = \tanh(Z_1)$. The chain rule gives, from the output back: 1. $\partial L / \partial \hat y = -2(y - \hat y)/n$ 2. $\partial L / \partial w_2 = A_1^{\top}(\partial L/\partial \hat y)$ 3. $\partial L / \partial A_1 = (\partial L/\partial \hat y)\, w_2^{\top}$ 4. $\partial L / \partial Z_1 = \partial L/\partial A_1 \odot (1 - A_1^2)$, since $\tanh'(z) = 1 - \tanh^2(z)$ 5. $\partial L / \partial W_1 = X^{\top}(\partial L/\partial Z_1)$ The bias slopes are the column sums of the same quantities. Each line reuses the one above it, which is why the backward pass costs no more than a forward pass. ::: ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A network is trained by **gradient descent**: forward pass, backward pass, a small step for every weight, repeated. - **Forward propagation** computes the prediction and keeps every value on the way. **Backpropagation** passes the error back through the same arrows and gives every weight its slope in one pass. - The activation enters the backward pass only as its slope. - **Check a hand-written gradient** against small nudges of each weight; here all 21 slopes agreed to 10 decimal places. - The loss can pause on a **plateau** before falling again, so a run stopped early can look no better than a straight line. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Replace tanh with ReLU: `A1 <- pmax(Z1, 0)` in `forward()`, and `d_Z1 <- d_A1 * (Z1 > 0)` in `backward()`. Run the check against small nudges again. Does it still agree? 2. Set `par$W1[] <- 0` before training. How many of the four hidden units end up different from each other, and why?
